title: Symphony no. 4 in E minor, mvt 4 (Allegro energico e passionato)
source_citations: Donald Tovey, Essays in Musical Analysis vol. I (1935)
Arnold Schoenberg, Style and Idea — 'Brahms the Progressive' (1947)
Walter Frisch, Brahms: The Four Symphonies (1996)

key_plan.role: Eight-bar chaconne ground bass (rising chromatic descent E–F#–G–A–A#–B–B–E), winds and brass chorale; modeled on Bach Cantata 150
Variations 1–11; the ground bass repeats 11 times with increasing rhythmic and motivic activity, all in E minor with Phrygian inflections
Variations 12–15; modal shift to E major, flute solo at var. 12 — the lyrical center of the movement
Return to E minor at var. 16; further variations build to climax (the bass line eventually emerges into the upper voices)
Più allegro coda (the boundary is loosely m. 253; exact count depends on edition). Final cadence in E minor.

notable_cadences.basis: Theme's closing half cadence onto V (B major)
Cadence preparing the major-mode pivot at variation 12
Cadence closing the major-mode variation group
Final perfect authentic cadence of movement (approximate measure — varies by edition)

characteristic_features: Chaconne / passacaglia form — 30+ variations on an 8-bar ground bass
Ground bass is itself a chromatic descent — Brahms's contribution to the lament-bass tradition (Purcell, Bach)
Modal shift to E major at variations 12–15 is the structural fulcrum
Schoenberg cited the work as an exemplar of 'developing variation'
common_omr_pitfalls: Late-Romantic orchestral score with 16+ parts — significant voice-conflation risk
Chromatic neighbor tones in the ground bass (A and A#) frequently misread as the same pitch by OMR
Variation boundaries are sometimes obscured by overlapping voicings — section boundaries in analysis may shift ±2 measures from edition to edition
_notes: Curated 2026-05-24. Measure counts approximate — Brahms's variation boundaries can shift by 1-2 measures across editions (Breitkopf, Eulenburg, Bärenreiter). Cross-check tolerance of ±2 should accommodate this. Major-mode variation group (vars. 12–15) is the most analytically distinctive feature and the strongest match-signal.
